42391314.headline: Testosterone therapy linked to lower death rates in men with low testosterone
42391314.summary: A registry study of 737 men, followed for almost nine years, also found that treatment changed how age related to the risk of dying.
body: Testosterone levels fall in some men as adults, a condition called adult-onset testosterone deficiency. It often occurs alongside weight gain, raised blood sugar and other features of what doctors call metabolic syndrome.

Researchers analysed a registry of 737 men with the condition who were followed for nearly nine years. Of these, 353 received long-acting testosterone injections (testosterone undecanoate) and 384 chose not to be treated.

Deaths were less common among the treated men. The team also found something unexpected. In treated men, the risk of dying rose with age in the usual pattern. In untreated men, age showed no clear link with death. Having type 2 diabetes did not change these results.

The authors suggest a possible reason: in untreated men, metabolic problems worsened and may have overshadowed the normal effect of age, while in treated men those risk factors improved. They present this as a possibility. The men chose for themselves whether to be treated, so the two groups may have differed in other ways.

42853362.headline: Not all sperm DNA damage is the same, researchers argue
42853362.summary: A new paper proposes mapping where and when the damage happens, to help explain male infertility and guide treatment.
body: Breaks in the DNA carried by sperm are linked to male fertility problems. Clinics usually report this damage as a single figure, known as sperm DNA fragmentation.

The authors argue that one figure hides important differences. They propose a "causal atlas" that would map when and where the damage arises, from the time sperm are formed, through their passage along the male reproductive tract, to ejaculation.

In their view the damage falls into two broad kinds. The first is "programmed", arising from faults while the sperm's DNA is being packaged or from cell death that starts but does not finish. The second is "acquired", caused by chemical attack, such as oxidative stress, during the sperm's journey.

The authors acknowledge that current tests cannot say for certain which kind of damage a man has or where it happened. They suggest that combining several complementary tests could help group patients more meaningfully and lead to more targeted treatments.

42851888.headline: War nightmares linked to physical symptoms among displaced Lebanese adults
42851888.summary: A survey of 294 people displaced during the 2024-2025 war found that depression explained part of the connection.
body: People who live through war often feel distress in their bodies as well as their minds, through pain, fatigue and other physical complaints. Doctors call this somatization.

Researchers surveyed 294 displaced Lebanese adults between October 2024 and March 2025. Their average age was about 25 and nearly three quarters were women. Participants reported how often they had nightmares about the war, along with symptoms of anxiety, depression and physical distress.

More frequent nightmares were linked with more anxiety, more depression and more physical symptoms. Part of the link between nightmares and physical symptoms ran through depression. Anxiety on its own did not play the same role. Nightmares were also linked to physical symptoms directly.

The study has limits. It measured everything at one point in time, so it cannot show what causes what, and participants were recruited through personal networks, which may not represent all displaced people. The authors say the findings point to a need for mental health care that addresses nightmares, mood and physical symptoms together.

42842184.headline: Review of spinal injection errors finds antiseptics behind the worst outcomes
42842184.summary: An analysis of 50 published reports from 1981 to 2025 looks at what happens when the wrong substance is given during spinal or epidural procedures.
body: Anaesthetists often give medicines through the spine, by epidural or spinal injection, for surgery, childbirth and pain relief. Rarely, the wrong substance is given by this route.

This review gathered published reports of such errors from 1981 to 2025. It found 50 reports covering 54 patients. Most involved the epidural route, and 73% of the patients were women. Atropine was the substance most often given by mistake, in six patients.
The most serious outcomes were permanent paralysis in four patients and death in four patients. These were mostly caused by antiseptic solution being injected by accident.

Using a recognised method for analysing human and system failures, the author found slips in routine skills and mix-ups between objects that look alike, as well as weaknesses in organisation, resources and supervision. The review concludes that hospitals could help prevent these events by improving safety procedures across teams. It is based on published case reports, so it cannot show how often such errors happen.

42841695.headline: Locally made heart stents perform as well as international ones in trials so far
42841695.summary: A review of four randomised trials with 2,793 patients found no consistent difference in safety or effectiveness.
body: A stent is a small mesh tube placed in a narrowed heart artery to keep it open. Newer designs use very thin metal struts and release medicine to help the artery heal. Locally manufactured versions of these stents are increasingly used in countries with a high burden of heart disease.

This review asked whether those locally made ultrathin stents work as well as established international brands. The authors searched five research databases up to December 2025 and found four randomised trials, including 2,793 patients.

Across the trials, the two types of stent had similar rates of serious heart problems, heart attacks, repeat procedures and blood clots in the stent. No consistent difference appeared in either direction.

The authors caution that only four trials exist and that they differed from one another. They call for larger studies with longer follow-up, and for monitoring of how the devices perform in everyday practice.

42859675.headline: Mixing cardio with strength training linked to a better blood sugar profile in diabetes
42859675.summary: A study of 185 adults at Thumbay Hospital, Ajman, found that physically active patients had a more favourable marker of sugar-related risk.
body: Two people with diabetes can have the same blood sugar readings and still differ in how much sugar attaches to their red blood cells. Doctors capture that difference with a measure called the haemoglobin glycation index, or HGI, which is used as a marker of cardiovascular risk and of how patients respond to treatment.

Researchers studied 185 adults with type 2 diabetes at Thumbay Hospital in Ajman. Of these, 98 were physically active and 87 were sedentary. After an overnight fast, the team measured each person's HGI along with signalling molecules released by muscle and fat.

Active participants had a lower HGI than sedentary ones, and the link remained after accounting for age, sex and body mass index. Among the active group, those who combined aerobic and resistance training had the most favourable results, although that subgroup was small, at 17 people.

The study looked at a single point in time, so it cannot show that exercise caused the difference. If follow-up studies confirm the findings, they could help doctors tailor exercise advice to individual patients.

42836380.headline: Two digital ways of measuring dental implants both prove accurate enough
42836380.summary: A study of 26 patients compared a camera-based technique with standard digital scanning for full-arch implants.
body: When a patient has lost all the teeth in one jaw, dentists can fix a full set of replacement teeth onto implants. To make teeth that fit, they must record the exact position of each implant. Traditionally this is done with a physical mould, but digital methods are now common.

This study compared two digital methods in 26 patients, each with four implants in a toothless upper jaw. One was a standard scan of the mouth. The other was photogrammetry, which calculates positions from images of special markers. Both were checked against a conventional mould.

Across the whole jaw, photogrammetry was slightly closer to the mould, with an average difference of 39.2 micrometres against 45.1 for the standard scan. It did better at the front of the mouth, while the standard scan did better at the back. Both stayed within the range considered acceptable for a good fit.

The authors note that the gap between the two methods is very small and may be no bigger than the error in the mould itself. They describe the result as a lead for further research, not proof that one method is better.

42835369.headline: Heavy TikTok use linked to distress, partly through feeling judged by age
42835369.summary: A survey of 855 Lebanese adults explored why addictive use of the app goes hand in hand with anxiety and depression.
body: Earlier research has linked compulsive use of TikTok with depression and anxiety, but the reasons are not well understood. This study tested one possible explanation: that heavy users feel more exposed to ageism, meaning being judged or treated unfairly because of their age.

Researchers surveyed 855 adults in Lebanon, with an average age of about 24. Around three quarters were women. Participants completed questionnaires on TikTok addiction symptoms, experiences of ageism and psychological distress. The main analysis used the 735 people who answered every question.

People with more signs of TikTok addiction reported more distress. They also reported more experiences of ageism, and that explained a small part of the link. Women, people with less education, those with a past mental health diagnosis and younger participants reported more distress.

The study captured one moment in time, so it cannot show cause and effect, and the role of ageism was small. The authors call for mental health and digital literacy programmes suited to the local culture.

42836184.headline: New laboratory-made compounds show promise against a target in brain and immune disease
42836184.summary: Two of the molecules blocked the enzyme PDE7A far more strongly than an older drug, in laboratory and computer tests.
body: PDE7A is an enzyme that helps control chemical signalling inside cells. Scientists see it as a possible target for treating inflammatory, autoimmune and neurodegenerative conditions, but strong and selective drugs against it have been hard to develop.

In this study, researchers designed and made two related families of new compounds and tested how well each one blocked the enzyme in the laboratory. They compared them with theophylline, an older medicine, and with a known experimental PDE7 blocker.

All of the new compounds blocked the enzyme. The two strongest performed about as well as the experimental blocker and were significantly more potent than theophylline. Computer simulations showed these two fitting tightly and stably into the enzyme, and computer predictions across 30 safety measures suggested a favourable profile.
These are early results from laboratory and computer work. The compounds have not been tested in animals or people, and the authors say the findings support developing them further.

42822610.headline: Fruit fly study shows two Alzheimer's proteins each weaken a cell-cleaning gene
42822610.summary: The effect grew as the flies aged, and one protein, amyloid-beta, had the stronger impact.
body: In Alzheimer's disease, two proteins build up in the brain: amyloid-beta and tau. Brain cells also lose some of their ability to clear away damaged proteins, a job done by a waste-disposal system inside the cell.

Researchers used fruit flies, a common stand-in for studying human brain disease, to ask how each protein affects a gene called UCH, which is a key part of that disposal system. They bred flies whose nerve cells produced either amyloid-beta or tau, and measured the gene's activity at 5, 15 and 25 days of adult life.

In flies making amyloid-beta, the gene's activity fell at all three ages, and the drop grew with age. In flies making tau, there was no significant change at 5 days, but a considerable decline at 15 and 25 days. Amyloid-beta had the larger effect at every age.
The findings come from flies, not people. The authors conclude that the two proteins each harm this gene independently, and suggest that treatments aimed at both may be worth considering.

42662413.headline: Tiny enzyme-like particles could calm the brain's immune system in Parkinson's disease
42662413.summary: A review examines how "nanozymes" might protect nerve cells, and what stands in the way of using them in patients.
body: Parkinson's disease is often described as a loss of nerve cells. Researchers increasingly see it also as a disorder of the brain's immune system, in which long-lasting inflammation, damaged cell power plants and a leaky barrier between blood and brain all speed up the damage.
This review sets out how nerve cells and immune cells communicate in health and in Parkinson's, and looks at treatments designed to restore the balance.

Its main focus is on nanozymes. These are extremely small engineered particles that behave like the body's natural enzymes. According to the studies reviewed, they can mop up harmful molecules, break down clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein, help strengthen the blood-brain barrier and steer immune cells towards a protective role. The authors also describe combining them with other tiny carriers to deliver drugs or genetic treatments.
This is a review of existing research, not a new trial. The authors discuss the challenges that remain before such approaches could be used to treat people.

42598601.headline: Heat treatment through a needle resolves gland disorder in patient who declined surgery
42598601.summary: A case report describes a 33-year-old woman whose calcium levels have stayed normal for three years after microwave ablation.
body: The parathyroid glands in the neck control calcium levels in the blood. When one develops a benign growth, it releases too much hormone and calcium rises, causing problems such as tiredness and muscle weakness. The standard treatment is surgery to remove the gland.

This report describes a 33-year-old woman with the condition who met the criteria for surgery but chose not to have it. Doctors used microwave ablation instead. Guided by ultrasound, they passed a needle into the growth and destroyed it with heat.

The procedure, carried out in October 2022, caused no complications. Her calcium and hormone levels returned to normal and her symptoms cleared. Three years later, they remain normal and she has not needed surgery.

This is the experience of one patient. The authors say it adds to growing evidence that microwave ablation can be an option for selected patients who cannot or do not want to have surgery, and that more research and long-term data are needed.

42303223.headline: Two types of replacement heart valve each have their own strengths, large review finds
42303223.summary: An analysis of 53 studies covering almost 158,000 patients compared the two main designs used without open-heart surgery.
body: A narrowed aortic valve can now be replaced without open-heart surgery. Doctors thread a new valve through a blood vessel in the leg and into the heart. Two main designs exist: one is expanded with a balloon, and the other expands on its own.
This review combined the results of 53 studies with 157,921 patients. Six were randomised trials and the rest were observational studies.

Balloon-expanded valves were linked with fewer deaths at one month and six months, fewer deaths from heart causes at one year, and a lower need for a permanent pacemaker. Self-expanding valves allowed blood to flow more freely, with lower pressure across the valve and a larger opening. Over the longer term, death rates and complications such as major bleeding and heart attack were similar.
The authors conclude that the choice of valve should be tailored to each patient. Because most of the studies were not randomised, they call for more trials with longer follow-up.

42269861.headline: Treating irregular heartbeat within a year of diagnosis linked to fewer relapses
42269861.summary: A review of 10 studies with 22,748 patients compared early and delayed catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation.
body: Atrial fibrillation is the most common heart rhythm disorder in the world. One treatment is catheter ablation, in which doctors thread a thin tube into the heart and treat the small areas of tissue that trigger the irregular beat.
This review asked whether timing matters. It combined 10 studies with 22,748 patients and compared those treated within 12 months of diagnosis with those treated later.

Patients who had the procedure early were less likely to see the irregular rhythm come back. They were also less likely to be admitted to hospital because of it, or to need an electric shock to reset the heartbeat. There was no significant difference in deaths, strokes, repeat ablation or overall hospital admissions.

The studies differed considerably from one another in their results on relapse, and some were observational. The authors say randomised trials are needed to confirm long-term benefits and to identify which patients gain most from early treatment.

42057369.headline: Loop-shaped RNA molecules show promise for detecting mouth cancer earlier
42057369.summary: A review of 29 studies found the markers were most accurate when measured in saliva and blood.
body: Mouth cancer is often found late, which is one reason survival remains poor. Researchers are looking for markers that could flag the disease earlier and help predict how it will progress.

One candidate is circular RNA, a type of genetic molecule that forms a closed loop. The loop makes it unusually stable, so it can be measured reliably in body fluids. This review brought together 29 studies of circular RNAs in oral squamous cell carcinoma, the most common mouth cancer.

Markers measured in tumour tissue were moderately accurate at identifying the cancer. Those measured in saliva and blood did better, reaching high accuracy in some studies. Certain circular RNAs were linked with poorer survival and others with better outcomes, and one found in tiny particles shed by cells independently predicted relapse and death.

The authors say these markers have strong potential, especially for tests based on a simple fluid sample. But the studies were small, varied and not confirmed across multiple centres, so they are not ready for routine use.

41902510.headline: Survey explores what shapes job satisfaction among radiography educators in the UAE
41902510.summary: Gender and level of education made a difference among the 40 academic radiographers who took part.
body: Academic radiographers both teach students and work with patients. In the UAE they face heavy workloads, occupational risks and the challenge of balancing two roles, and their job satisfaction affects patient care and whether staff stay.
Researchers surveyed 40 academic radiographers in the UAE using an online questionnaire covering motivation, career progression and workplace benefits.

Gender and education level were linked to satisfaction. Women reported higher satisfaction than men with salary, workload and respect at work. Those with a PhD reported more freedom to make decisions and more harmony at work than those with a bachelor's degree. Staff at private academic institutions received more rewards based on skills, and those in private hospitals reported better recognition and working environments.

The survey was small, with 40 participants, and captured one point in time. The authors recommend policies that take gender into account, fair promotion, and careful workload management to improve retention.

41817655.headline: Glowing nanoparticles could help detect and treat motor neurone disease, review suggests
41817655.summary: Researchers examine how "quantum dots" might be used to diagnose ALS earlier and deliver medicines more precisely.
body: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, is a fatal disease that destroys the nerve cells controlling movement. It remains hard to detect early.

This review looks at quantum dots, particles so small they are measured in billionths of a metre. They glow when light is shone on them, which makes them useful as tags for spotting specific molecules.

According to the review, quantum dots could be designed to attach to proteins or genetic material linked to ALS, allowing these to be identified and monitored. They could be built into sensitive tests that detect signs of the disease in body fluids. They can also carry medicines to their target, which may limit build-up elsewhere in the body and reduce side effects.

The article is a review of existing research and describes what may become possible; it does not report a new treatment. The authors cover progress in research, clinical trials and patents, along with the challenges that remain.

41576963.headline: Low doses of pomegranate extract help dental stem cells turn into bone-forming cells
41576963.summary: In laboratory tests, higher doses had the opposite effect, pointing to the importance of getting the amount right.
body: Gum disease can destroy the bone and tissue that hold teeth in place. Researchers are looking for ways to help the body rebuild them, including with natural plant compounds.

In this study, scientists took stem cells from the ligament around extracted human molars and grew them in the laboratory. They then exposed the cells to different concentrations of pomegranate extract while encouraging them to develop into bone-forming cells.

One of the low concentrations tested gave the best results. Cells showed more activity in genes linked to bone formation and cell growth than untreated cells. Higher concentrations were less helpful: one produced the weakest bone-related response and the highest level of an inflammation signal, and at a higher concentration still, fewer cells survived.

The work was done on cells in the laboratory, not in patients. The authors conclude that pomegranate extract, at the right dose, may be a promising natural aid for regenerating tissue around teeth, and that further studies are needed to test its clinical potential.

42814432.headline: An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023
42814432.summary: A global analysis covering 204 countries and territories shows the causes vary widely by age and region.
body: Heart failure is a condition in which the heart cannot pump blood as well as the body needs. This analysis, part of the Global Burden of Disease Study, estimated how common it is around the world using data from 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
It estimated 56 million cases worldwide in 2023. Heart failure became more common with age in every location.

The causes varied. Among older adults, the two most common were narrowed heart arteries and long-term high blood pressure. In children and young adults, heart defects present at birth and rheumatic heart disease were common causes. Heart failure related to alcohol peaked in middle age. Some causes were concentrated in particular regions, such as rheumatic heart disease in parts of Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, and Chagas disease in Latin America.

The figures are estimates built from many data sources and carry a range of uncertainty. The authors expect the burden to grow as populations age, and note that most causes can be prevented by tackling high blood pressure, excessive alcohol use and tobacco.

42689187.headline: Search for cancer drugs in marine microbes yields a method, though not yet a medicine
42689187.summary: A compound picked out by computer screening killed some cancer cells in the laboratory but did not block its intended target.
body: Many medicines began as natural products made by microbes. In this study, researchers built a step-by-step process to search microbial products for ones that might block the proteasome, a piece of cell machinery that is an established target for cancer drugs.

They started with computer screening to predict which natural products would attach to the target. One compound, marinacarboline C, came out as a top candidate. The team then made it in the laboratory and tested it on five types of cancer cell and one non-cancer cell type.

The compound was most toxic to one of the five cancer cell types. But when tested directly in breast cancer cells, it did not significantly reduce the activity of the proteasome, so it did not work in the way the computer had predicted.

The authors present the study as a proof of concept for the search method, not a new drug. They also identified related gene clusters in other microbes that may produce similar compounds, as leads for future work.

42856932.headline: Cracking sunflower seeds with the front teeth may wear notches in them
42856932.summary: A review of eight published articles found tooth wear was the main dental finding linked to the habit.
body: Eating sunflower seeds in their shells, and cracking them open with the teeth, is a common habit in many cultures. This review gathered what has been published about its effects on the mouth.

The authors searched six research databases for studies published up to August 2026. They found eight articles: two surveys, three reports of individual patients, two small series of cases and one narrative review.

The main finding was loss of tooth surface, appearing as characteristic notches on the biting edges of the front teeth. Less often, the articles reported chipped teeth, sensitivity, receding gums and inflammation around a dental implant caused by trapped food. Jaw joint symptoms and sore chewing muscles appeared in just one series of cases.

The evidence is thin. Most of it comes from individual cases, and the authors stress that it is not enough to show the seeds cause the damage. They call for larger studies that follow people over time.

42798116.headline: Patients are more satisfied when their cancer nurse navigators are more skilled
42798116.summary: A study at a cancer centre in Cairo involved 65 nurse navigators and 404 patients.
body: A cancer diagnosis brings a maze of appointments, tests and decisions. Oncology nurse navigators are nurses who guide patients through it, and the role is still uncommon in Egypt.

Researchers studied 65 nurse navigators and 404 patients at a major cancer hospital in Cairo. The nurses completed a questionnaire measuring their core skills, and patients rated their satisfaction with their navigator.

Patient satisfaction was high overall. Navigators with higher skill scores tended to have more satisfied patients, and the link was strong. It was strongest for expert navigation skills and for coordinating care. Nurses' skill scores varied with their age, education, experience and how often they received training.

The study measured everything at one point in time and compared averages for each nurse, so it cannot show that better skills cause higher satisfaction for an individual patient. The authors say the findings support continued training and stronger nurse navigation services.

42788872.headline: Testosterone therapy linked to lower "bad" cholesterol in men with low testosterone
42788872.summary: In a long-running registry, cholesterol and blood fats fell in treated men and gradually rose in untreated men.
body: Men whose testosterone falls in adulthood have higher rates of heart disease and death. This study examined whether treating the deficiency is linked to changes in blood fats, which are major risk factors for heart disease.

Researchers analysed a registry of men with adult-onset testosterone deficiency, 409 treated with long-acting testosterone injections and 415 untreated, followed for a median of about 13 years. To avoid confusing the picture, they looked only at men whose cholesterol-lowering medication stayed the same throughout.

In treated men, LDL cholesterol (often called "bad" cholesterol) and triglycerides, another blood fat, fell significantly, mostly in the first two years. In untreated men they rose. The pattern held whether or not the men were taking statins. Men who started with higher levels saw bigger drops.

The data come from a registry, not a randomised trial, and the groups differed at the start. Drawing on other published research, the authors estimate that the fall in LDL cholesterol could correspond to around a 40% lower relative risk of cardiovascular disease.

42852021.headline: One in five parents of babies in intensive care screens positive for anxiety
42852021.summary: A pilot study at Thumbay University Hospital, Ajman, also found signs of depression and post-traumatic stress among parents.
body: Having a newborn in intensive care is frightening for parents. This pilot study set out to measure how many show signs of psychological distress.

Researchers gave questionnaires to 82 parents of babies admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at Thumbay University Hospital in Ajman between March and July 2025. The questionnaires screen for symptoms of anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder.

In all, 22% of parents screened positive for anxiety symptoms, 13.4% for depression and 9.8% for post-traumatic stress. Mothers were more likely than fathers to screen positive for depression, and parents aged 30 or under were more likely than older parents to screen positive for post-traumatic stress. The most common ways of coping were religious or spiritual practices, followed by physical or behavioural methods.

This was a small pilot study, and a positive screen is not a diagnosis. The authors urge caution because few parents screened positive in each group. They say the results support considering mental health screening and culturally appropriate support for parents.

42784603.headline: Waterpipe smoke triggers a survival response in lung cells that may be an early step towards cancer
42784603.summary: Laboratory tests on human airway cells found DNA damage, inflammation signals and markers linked to cancer stem cells.
body: Waterpipe smoking, also known as shisha, is a growing health concern worldwide, but its effects on the cells lining the airways are not fully understood.

Researchers exposed healthy human airway cells in the laboratory to condensed waterpipe smoke. High concentrations killed the cells. At a low concentration, the cells largely survived, and the team investigated how.

They found that the smoke switched on autophagy, a process in which a cell breaks down and recycles its own parts to cope with stress. When the researchers blocked this process, more cells died, suggesting it was protecting them. The exposed cells also showed DNA damage, produced more inflammation signals, and displayed markers associated with cancer stem cells.
The experiments were done on cells in the laboratory, not in people. The authors suggest that this survival response may be an early event linking waterpipe smoke to lung cancer.

42840142.headline: Low oxygen inside tumours may link cancer's toughest cells to a weakened immune response
42840142.summary: A review of 14 studies proposes a framework that could point to new treatment targets, but says it still needs testing in patients.
body: The inside of a tumour is often short of oxygen. Tumours also contain cancer stem cells, a small group of hardy cells thought to drive regrowth and spread, and they tend to suppress the immune system around them. These three features have mostly been studied separately.
This review asked whether low oxygen ties them together. From 1,569 records published between 2010 and early 2026, the authors selected 14 studies that examined all three in the same experiments.

Low-oxygen conditions were repeatedly linked with more cancer stem cells, greater ability to spread, weaker immune attack and resistance to treatment. The authors describe several ways this happens, including immune cells that normally kill tumour cells working less well, and other immune cells being drawn into supporting the cancer stem cells.

Most of the evidence came from laboratory experiments. The authors describe their model as a framework for understanding, not proof of a universal pathway, and say it needs to be confirmed in human tumours.

42835725.headline: A donor's metabolic health may affect how well sperm survive freezing and handling
42835725.summary: A review spanning animals and humans proposes tailoring sperm processing to the donor's hormonal and metabolic profile.
body: Sperm used in assisted reproduction and in animal breeding are often cooled, frozen, sorted and thawed. These steps are stressful for the cells, and some samples cope much better than others.

This review argues that part of the difference lies in the donor's metabolic and hormonal health. It brings together evidence, across several species, on insulin resistance, hormones released by body fat, and vitamin D and calcium signalling.

According to the review, metabolic strain is associated with sperm that are more vulnerable to chemical damage and handle energy differently, which magnifies harm during cooling, freezing and sorting. Fat-derived hormones and vitamin D signalling also appear to influence how sperm move and survive.

The authors propose grouping donors by metabolic profile and adjusting processing methods to suit. They are clear that this is a proposal: the evidence supports further investigation, and they call for trials designed to test the idea. They note it is especially relevant to veterinary practice, such as artificial insemination centres and semen banks.

42786472.headline: New self-setting tooth filling outperforms a light-cured rival in laboratory tests
42786472.summary: Researchers compared the two materials in 60 extracted teeth, looking at stress on the tooth, the seal at the edges and tiny leaks.
body: Most white fillings are hardened with a blue light. As they set they shrink slightly, which can pull on the walls of the tooth and leave small gaps where bacteria can enter. A newer type of filling material sets by itself, with no light, and has been proposed as an alternative to traditional silver amalgam.

In this laboratory study, researchers prepared large cavities in 60 human premolars that had been extracted for orthodontic reasons. Half were filled with the self-setting material and half with a widely used light-cured material.

Teeth filled with the self-setting material flexed inward less, both five minutes and 24 hours after filling. After the teeth were put through repeated temperature changes and chewing forces to imitate ageing, that material also sealed better at the edges and showed less microscopic leakage.

The tests were done on extracted teeth in the laboratory. The authors say the results indicate the material's potential as an alternative for large fillings in premolars, but it has not been compared in patients here.

42828068.headline: AI can suggest new uses for old drugs, but the suggestions need better checks, review warns
42828068.summary: Researchers propose a step-by-step framework that puts safety and biological evidence ahead of prediction scores.
body: Finding a new use for a medicine that already exists can be faster and cheaper than developing one from scratch. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to scan data and predict which existing drugs might work for other diseases.
This critical review surveys the AI methods in use and asks how far their predictions can be trusted.

The authors found that these tools can greatly increase the number of candidate drugs identified. But they share common weaknesses. Many studies focus on prediction scores and rankings, with little attention to how the drug would work in the body, whether the evidence shows cause and effect, what dose would be safe, or whether the result holds up outside the original data.

To address this, the authors propose a sequence of steps: predict candidates, map how the drug would act, weigh whether the link is plausible, assess safety and toxicity, check real-world safety reports and patient data, and have pharmacology experts review the result. The framework is a proposal and has not yet been tested in practice.

42792068.headline: Antibiotics may help in severe gum disease, but should be used selectively
42792068.summary: A review of existing reviews found benefit for one antibiotic combination and too little evidence for another.
body: Severe gum disease damages the tissue and bone that support the teeth and is a major health problem worldwide. The main treatment is deep cleaning below the gumline. Dentists sometimes add antibiotic tablets, but how much this helps has been uncertain.

This study is an "umbrella review", meaning it reviewed earlier systematic reviews. It looked for those published from June 2018 to June 2026 that covered the two most severe stages of gum disease under the current classification. Only two met the criteria, and they drew heavily on the same original studies.

One review reported moderately reliable evidence that adding amoxicillin plus metronidazole to deep cleaning improved gum attachment and reduced pocket depth more than cleaning alone. The other found too little evidence to support routinely adding azithromycin.

With only two overlapping reviews available, the evidence is limited. The authors conclude that antibiotics should be used selectively, based on the individual patient and with care to avoid overuse, and not as a routine addition.

42511740.headline: Low oxygen changes how pancreatic cancer cells respond to an emerging way of killing tumours
42511740.summary: Laboratory tests on three cell lines found large differences between them, with some resisting treatment when oxygen was scarce.
body: Pancreatic cancer is hard to treat, in part because its tumours are starved of oxygen and resist standard therapies. Researchers are exploring ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron, as a way to kill cancer cells that survive other treatments.
This study asked how low oxygen affects that approach. The team treated three types of pancreatic cancer cell in the laboratory with drugs that trigger ferroptosis, under normal and very low oxygen.

The three cell types behaved differently. One was the most sensitive. Another resisted the drugs, especially in low oxygen. The cells also sent out different signals when treated: the sensitive type switched on a set of genes associated with alerting the immune system, particularly in low oxygen, a second type released a broader range of inflammatory signals, and the resistant type barely responded.

The work was done on cells grown in the laboratory. The authors say it reveals complex interactions between this form of cell death, the immune system and the tumour's environment, which future treatments would need to take into account.

42505207.headline: After lung cancer surgery in patients over 80, major complications are linked to shorter survival
42505207.summary: A study of 88 patients found blood transfusion was a key risk factor and keyhole surgery was linked to better survival.
body: More people in their eighties are now offered surgery for lung cancer, but they are at higher risk of complications. This study looked at which factors predict serious problems and how those problems affect survival.
Researchers reviewed the records of 88 patients aged 80 or over who had part of a lung removed for cancer.

Major complications occurred in 24 patients, or 27.3%. Needing a blood transfusion around the time of surgery was an independent risk factor for major complications, and was also linked to shorter survival. Patients who had major complications lived for a significantly shorter time overall. Those who had minimally invasive, or keyhole, surgery survived significantly longer.

The study looked back at past records from a small group, so it shows associations and cannot prove cause. The authors suggest that keyhole approaches and steps to reduce the need for transfusion may help improve outcomes in this high-risk group.

42098650.headline: Zebrafish test of an oxygen-boosting cancer drug shows only mild effects
42098650.summary: Researchers tested the experimental compound ITPP on human pancreatic tumours grown in zebrafish.
body: Pancreatic tumours are short of oxygen, which helps them resist treatment. An experimental compound called ITPP is designed to counter this by helping red blood cells release more oxygen.

To watch its early effects, researchers implanted human pancreatic cancer cells into zebrafish, whose transparent bodies allow tumours and blood vessels to be seen in real time. They tested the compound alone and with a standard chemotherapy combination.

The effects were mild. More tumours had vessels carrying red blood cells, hinting at better-working vessels, but the structure of the vessels did not change. The compound did not alter how well the chemotherapy killed cancer cells. Treated tumours did show more cell death, apparently through an indirect effect on the tumour's surroundings.

The authors report that they could not detect major effects, possibly because tumours in this zebrafish model are not short of oxygen in the first place. They see this as a shortcoming of the model for testing oxygen-related drugs and suggest ways to adapt it.

42067504.headline: Being over 80 does not by itself raise the risk of complications after lung cancer surgery
42067504.summary: A study of 180 patients in their seventies and eighties found general fitness, lung function and a blood protein level mattered more than age.
body: Lung cancer becomes more common with age, and older patients are generally considered more likely to have complications after major lung surgery. This study examined whether age itself is the problem.
Researchers reviewed 180 consecutive patients with lung cancer who had surgery. Of these, 141 were in their seventies and 39 in their eighties.

Complications occurred in 67 patients, or 37.2%, and 1.6% died within 30 days. The rate of complications did not differ between the two age groups. Three other factors independently predicted major complications: being less able to carry out daily activities, reduced lung function on a breathing test, and a low level of the blood protein albumin, which can be a sign of poor nutrition.

The study looked back at past records, and only 39 patients were over 80. The authors conclude that age over 80 was not an independent risk factor, and that a patient's general condition gives a better guide to risk.

42123455.headline: Tackling low oxygen in pancreatic tumours could help immunotherapy work, review argues
42123455.summary: The authors say treatment should be matched to how oxygen-starved each patient's tumour is.
body: Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, with a five-year survival rate of 13%. Immunotherapy drugs known as checkpoint inhibitors have transformed the treatment of several cancers, but in pancreatic cancer they have had a negligible effect.

This review argues that severe shortage of oxygen inside the tumour is a central reason. Low oxygen reshapes the tumour's surroundings into a harsh environment that keeps immune cells out and suppresses those that get in.

The authors survey treatments that target low oxygen directly or indirectly, including drugs that block the cell's oxygen-sensing machinery, drugs that become active only in low-oxygen tissue, and approaches that improve blood vessels and oxygen delivery. No such treatment is currently combined with immunotherapy in routine care.

One obstacle, they suggest, is treating all patients alike. Tumours are not equally short of oxygen, and patients with more oxygen-starved tumours tend to have worse survival. The authors propose using gene-based tests to identify these tumours, so that treatment can be targeted. This is a review of existing research and the approach remains to be proven.

42064067.headline: An immune signalling molecule on melanoma cells behaves differently as the cancer advances
42064067.summary: Laboratory work identifies a protein called PSAP that responds in opposite ways in early and advanced skin cancer cells.
body: Interleukin-15 is a molecule that normally helps activate the immune system. Melanoma cells, from the most serious type of skin cancer, carry it on their surface, in forms that differ between early tumours and those that have spread.

Researchers investigated what happens when the form anchored in the cell membrane is stimulated by its partner molecule. They analysed gene activity data from melanoma patients and measured protein changes in melanoma cells grown in the laboratory.

In patient data, high levels of interleukin-15 went together with immune activation, inflammation and a process that helps cancer cells become mobile. In the cell experiments, most of the proteins that changed did so in opposite directions in early-stage and advanced cells. One protein, PSAP, stood out as the most consistent: it rose in early melanoma cells and fell in advanced ones.

The study is laboratory research on cells and patient datasets, and does not test a treatment. The authors say it identifies PSAP as a stage-specific player that may influence how melanoma progresses.

41884789.headline: Age alone need not rule out surgery for a rare type of pancreatic tumour
41884789.summary: A study of 171 patients found that those aged 70 and over did as well in the short term as younger patients.
body: Non-functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours are a rare type of pancreatic tumour that does not produce excess hormones. They are being found more often, especially in older adults, because of the wider use of body scans. Surgery to remove them carries a high risk of complications, and it has been unclear how well older patients cope.
Researchers reviewed 171 patients who had this surgery at one institution between 2003 and 2023. Of these, 129 were under 70 and 42 were 70 or older.

The older patients had more heart conditions (62% against 30%) and lung conditions (15% against 5%). Even so, short-term results did not differ significantly between the groups. That included leaks from the pancreas, bleeding, length of hospital stay and deaths within 30 days. The tumours themselves were also similar in stage and aggressiveness.
The study looked back at past records from a single institution and covers short-term outcomes only. The authors conclude that surgery appears to be a safe option for patients of 70 and over.

41915668.headline: Study maps which HPV types are most common among women in the UAE
41915668.summary: Testing of 229 cervical screening samples found the virus in 96, including some with normal-looking cells.
body: Human papillomavirus, or HPV, is a common infection, and certain "high-risk" types can lead to cervical cancer. Knowing which types circulate locally helps in planning screening and vaccination.

Researchers analysed 229 cervical screening samples from women aged 20 to 55 attending Thumbay University Hospital and other hospitals in the UAE between January 2024 and January 2025. Alongside the usual examination of cells, they used a genetic test to identify the specific HPV types present.

HPV was found in 96 samples, and many carried more than one type: 191 were detected in all, of which 137 were high-risk types. Types 53, 16, 68, 66, 31 and 35 were among the most common high-risk types. Notably, 21% of samples whose cells looked normal tested positive for high-risk types.

The samples came from women attending hospital clinics, so the results may not reflect all women in the UAE. The authors say the findings highlight the value of genetic HPV testing in screening, and provide a baseline for assessing the impact of vaccination.

41908948.headline: New compounds kill the leishmaniasis parasite more effectively than a current drug in lab tests
41908948.summary: The lead molecule works by cutting off the parasite's supply of folate, tests showed.
body: Leishmaniasis is caused by parasites spread by the bite of sandflies. It ranges from skin sores to a fatal illness affecting internal organs, and more than 20 species of the parasite cause it.

Researchers designed and made 16 new compounds by joining two chemical structures already known to have biological activity. They tested them in the laboratory against two life stages of the species Leishmania major.

Several compounds were potent. The best, labelled 5b, was significantly more effective against both stages of the parasite than miltefosine, a drug currently used to treat the disease. Adding folate back into the experiment cancelled out the compound's effect, which confirmed that it works by blocking the parasite's use of this vitamin. Computer modelling supported this explanation and predicted that the compounds have properties suitable for a medicine.

These are early laboratory results, and the compounds have not been tested in animals or people. The authors say they offer a promising new chemical starting point for developing drugs against the disease.

41859341.headline: New compounds damage the DNA of leukaemia cells and work better alongside other targeted drugs
41859341.summary: In laboratory tests, the lead molecule blocked two enzymes that cancer cells need to copy their DNA.
body: Cancer cells divide rapidly, and to do so they must constantly unwind and copy their DNA. Enzymes called topoisomerases make this possible, and several established cancer drugs work by blocking them.
Researchers made a new series of compounds and tested them on four types of cancer cell in the laboratory, including two types of leukaemia.

Three compounds were the most potent at stopping leukaemia cells from growing. The lead compound, labelled 7e, blocked both main types of topoisomerase. Treated cells stalled while copying their DNA, showed signs of DNA damage and went on to self-destruct. When the compounds were combined with drugs that stop cancer cells repairing such damage, the effect on one type of leukaemia cell was much stronger than expected from either alone. Combining them with a different kind of repair-blocking drug added little.
The work was done on cells in the laboratory, and the compounds have not been tested in animals or people. The authors say the results point to possible value in combination treatments for leukaemia.

41497768.headline: Two-pronged compound stays effective against breast cancer cells when oxygen is low
41497768.summary: In laboratory tests it outperformed a standard chemotherapy drug under the low-oxygen conditions that often make tumours resistant.
body: Many aggressive tumours are short of oxygen, and this makes them harder to treat. Two proteins help tumours thrive in these conditions: one helps them grow new blood vessels and the other helps them cope with the acidity that low oxygen creates.
Researchers designed and made a series of new compounds intended to block both proteins at once. The most powerful, labelled 4a, blocked each of them at very low concentrations.

Tested on breast cancer cells in the laboratory, the compound remained highly active whether oxygen was normal or low. In low oxygen it was more potent than doxorubicin, a widely used chemotherapy drug. It stopped cells from dividing, triggered self-destruction in more than half of them, and reduced their ability to move. Computer predictions suggested it has properties suitable for a medicine.
These are early results from one type of cancer cell in the laboratory and from computer modelling. The compound has not been tested in animals or people.

41471364.headline: New compound blocks two growth signals and selectively targets breast cancer cells in the lab
41471364.summary: It matched or exceeded an established cancer drug in tests on cells, while largely sparing normal breast cells.
body: Tumours rely on signals that tell them to grow, form new blood vessels and spread. Two of the proteins that pass on those signals are called VEGFR-2 and c-Met. Blocking both together is considered a promising strategy.
Researchers designed and made a series of new compounds intended to block both, and tested them on breast, prostate and lung cancer cells in the laboratory.

Five compounds strongly blocked both proteins. They were most toxic to breast cancer cells. One, labelled 11b, was highly selective, harming breast cancer cells much more than normal breast cells, and was as potent as or more potent than sorafenib, an established cancer drug. It halted cell division and triggered self-destruction in nearly half of the cancer cells. Computer modelling showed it fitting stably into both proteins.
The work was done on cells in the laboratory, and the compound has not been tested in animals or people. The authors see it as a strong candidate for developing a targeted breast cancer treatment.

41305011.headline: New compound shows activity against a wide range of cancer cells, including leukaemia
41305011.summary: Screened at the US National Cancer Institute, it blocked an enzyme cells need to manage their DNA about as well as an existing drug.
body: Topoisomerase II is an enzyme that untangles DNA so that cells can copy it and divide. Cancer cells depend on it heavily, and it is the target of several chemotherapy drugs.
Researchers designed and made a new series of compounds and sent them for testing against the US National Cancer Institute's panel of cancer cell lines.

Several compounds were active. One, labelled 8c, stood out, stopping the growth of a broad range of cancer cell types at low concentrations. The compounds also showed moderate to good activity against two types of leukaemia cell. Further tests showed that 8c damaged DNA, stalled cells while they were copying it, and led them to self-destruct. It blocked topoisomerase II in a dose-dependent way, comparable to etoposide, an established chemotherapy drug.

The results come from laboratory tests on cells. The authors describe the compound as a promising starting point to be refined further in cancer drug development, and it has not been tested in animals or people.

40871384.headline: Antibiotic-resistance genes found in every multidrug-resistant bacterium tested in northern UAE
40871384.summary: Researchers screened 3,670 clinical samples and examined 249 resistant bacteria in detail.
body: Some bacteria carry genes that let them destroy important antibiotics, including penicillin-type drugs and carbapenems, which doctors often reserve for serious infections. Tracking these genes helps hospitals understand and contain resistance.

Researchers examined 3,670 samples from patients at hospitals and clinics in the northern regions of the UAE. From these they isolated 249 bacteria resistant to multiple drugs, belonging to five species including E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, and tested them for six resistance genes.

Three of the genes, which give resistance to penicillin-type antibiotics, were detected in all of the multidrug-resistant bacteria. One of them, known as CTX-M, was the most common, especially in E. coli. Genes giving resistance to carbapenems were found in a few Klebsiella and Acinetobacter samples. Many bacteria carried two or more resistance genes together.

The study describes which genes are present and does not track how patients fared. The authors say the findings show the importance of genetic testing for monitoring and controlling drug-resistant bacteria.

40820991.headline: Fresh key lime oil shows anti-ageing potential for skin in laboratory tests
40820991.summary: Oil from fresh fruit outperformed oil from dried fruit at blocking enzymes that break down the skin's support proteins.
body: Demand for natural skincare is growing, and cosmetic companies are looking to plant extracts with anti-wrinkle properties. Skin stays firm and elastic thanks to two proteins, collagen and elastin, which are gradually broken down by enzymes as skin ages.

Researchers analysed the essential oils of fresh and dried key lime fruit, identified their chemical components, and tested how well each oil blocked the two enzymes in the laboratory. They also measured antioxidant activity.

Oil from fresh fruit blocked both enzymes well and was more effective than oil from dried fruit. It also had stronger antioxidant activity, suggesting that fresh fruit retains more of the active compounds. Computer modelling indicated that the oil's three main components fit well into the enzymes.

These are laboratory and computer results. The oil was not tested on human skin, so its effect in a real skincare product is not yet known. The authors suggest key lime oil could be a promising natural ingredient for anti-ageing formulations.

40667500.headline: Tiny particles made from a corn protein boost a painkiller's effect when applied to the skin
40667500.summary: In rats, the new formulation reduced inflammation more than the drug alone and did not irritate the skin.
body: Applying an anti-inflammatory drug to the skin can treat a problem where it occurs while limiting side effects elsewhere in the body. The challenge is getting enough of the drug through the skin.
Researchers loaded the anti-inflammatory drug dexketoprofen into nanoparticles made from zein, a protein found in corn. They tested different recipes to find the best one.

The chosen formulation captured about 92% of the drug in smooth, round particles roughly 92 nanometres across, far smaller than a human cell. When tested on rats with paw swelling, it produced significantly greater anti-inflammatory effect than the drug applied on its own. Examination of the rats' skin under the microscope showed no irritation.

The study was carried out in rats, and the formulation has not been tested in people. The authors say zein nanoparticles are a promising way to deliver the drug through the skin, with potential for treating inflammatory skin conditions.

40661854.headline: Bitter orange fruit and leaves contain compounds that block enzymes linked to several diseases
40661854.summary: Laboratory analysis suggests that waste from the fruit could be a source of antioxidants and supplements.
body: Citrus fruits are widely used in food, medicines and cosmetics. Bitter orange is one of them, and much of the plant is discarded as waste.

Researchers prepared extracts from bitter orange fruits and leaves and identified their chemical components, which they report had not been done before for this type of extract. They then tested the extracts in the laboratory for antioxidant activity and for their ability to block several enzymes.

The fruit and leaf extracts had different chemical make-ups. Both showed the potential to block enzymes involved in nerve signalling, which are targets in Alzheimer's disease research; an enzyme involved in skin pigmentation; and enzymes that break down starch and sugar, which are relevant to diabetes. Computer modelling supported the results and pointed to the compounds likely to be responsible, including one called lupeol found mainly in the leaves.

These are laboratory and computer findings. The extracts have not been tested in animals or people. The authors conclude that bitter orange waste could be a useful source of antioxidants and supplements.

40563638.headline: Drug that switches on in low oxygen helps kill breast cancer cells and exposes them to immune attack
40563638.summary: Laboratory tests showed evofosfamide worked better in the low-oxygen conditions where cancer cells usually resist treatment.
body: Parts of many tumours are starved of oxygen. Cancer cells in these areas tend to be more aggressive, resist treatment and hide from the immune system.

Evofosfamide is a drug designed to exploit this. It is inactive until it reaches low-oxygen tissue, where it turns into a compound that damages DNA. Researchers tested it on two types of breast cancer cell in the laboratory, under normal and low oxygen.

The drug killed more cancer cells in low oxygen than in normal oxygen, and the cells showed clear signs of self-destruction. It also restored a set of immune alarm signals that low oxygen normally switches off in these cells. As a result, natural killer cells, a type of immune cell, were able to attack and kill the cancer cells.
The experiments were done on cells in the laboratory, not in patients. The authors say the findings underline the drug's potential to make oxygen-starved tumours more vulnerable to treatment.

40074018.headline: Review charts fifteen years of progress on a promising target for new tuberculosis drugs
40074018.summary: The enzyme DprE1 is essential for building the wall of the tuberculosis bacterium, and blocking it kills the microbe.
body: Drug-resistant strains of tuberculosis continue to spread, and they are a serious global health threat. New medicines that work in different ways from existing ones are needed.
One promising target is an enzyme called DprE1, which the tuberculosis bacterium needs in order to build key components of its protective cell wall. Without it, the bacterium dies.

This review describes the compounds reported over the past fifteen years that block the enzyme. Its potential as a drug target first emerged from large-scale screening of chemicals, and since then compounds with many different chemical structures have been found to act on it. The authors group them by how they attach to the enzyme: some form a permanent chemical bond with it and others bind without one. They also cover the methods chemists use to make these compounds.
The article is a review of published research and does not report new experiments or a new medicine.

39729399.headline: Low oxygen and altered metabolism go hand in hand in breast tumours, depending on tumour type
39729399.summary: An analysis of data from more than 2,000 breast tumours suggests the relationship could matter for treatment.
body: Tumours often outgrow their blood supply and run short of oxygen. It is known that this changes how cancer cells use sugar, but its effect on the rest of their metabolism, the chemical reactions that keep cells alive, has been less clear.
Researchers analysed data from more than 2,000 breast tumours. They scored each one for signs of low oxygen and for the activity of 90 metabolic pathways.

Low oxygen was very strongly associated with a more aggressive metabolic profile. But the relationship was not the same everywhere. Breast tumours fall into three metabolic types, and the pattern of links between low oxygen and metabolism was specific to each. Experiments on cancer cells using drugs that block metabolism supported this. In one of the three types, low oxygen also appeared to be connected with the tumour's ability to evade the immune system.

The study is based mainly on analysis of existing tumour data, with supporting laboratory experiments. The authors say it reveals a complex interplay that may have implications for breast cancer treatment.
